text: As Microsoft pours billions into artificial intelligence, the company has offered buyouts to about 60,000 employees. The work force was already on edge. Credit... Tara Anand Supported by By Emmy Martin Reporting from San Francisco Within an hour of Microsoft’s announcement of buyouts last week, employees rushed to an internal site to see whether they had been offered one. So many people were checking at once that employees speculated on the company’s internal social network that the site had buckled under the traffic. The offer, extended to about 60,000 employees , or more than a quarter of Microsoft’s work force, was the largest in the company’s history. It was also the company’s second buyout this year, and another shock to a work force grappling with big changes brought on by artificial intelligence. For years, Microsoft occupied a distinct position among the tech industry’s biggest companies. While its pay packages often lagged behind Silicon Valley rivals like Google and Meta, employees said, the company countered with strong benefits and a reputation for stability. As recently as September, Forbes ranked Microsoft the world’s best employer for the third straight year. But the tech industry’s A.I. race is upending many workplaces, Microsoft included. The buyout offer, said six Microsoft employees who spoke on the condition of anonymity, landed on workers strained by mounting expectations to use A.I., stagnant pay and a growing sense that their jobs were no longer secure. Though Microsoft is doing better financially than most of its peers, it is clearly shifting its spending priorities. Two days after the buyouts were announced, the Redmond, Wash., company reported a 32 percent jump in quarterly profit, to $36.6 billion, on revenue of $92.3 billion. Its capital spending, largely on data centers, rose 30 percent to $45.2 billion, and the company said it expected to spend roughly $170 billion this year. The fear among many workers now is what comes next, and some have begun organizing. Before the buyout offer, a group of current and former employees circulated an open letter among colleagues accusing the company of pursuing A.I. with a “speed-at-all-costs” ethos. It called on Microsoft to involve employees in decisions about how A.I. is built and used, and to stop tying A.I. use to rewards or reprimands. Thank you for your patience while we verify access.
